sentences.text: Torosaurus was a massive ceratopsid that measured between 7.5 and 9 meters in length and weighed approximately 8 metric tons, though estimates range up to 11 metric tons.
This animal possessed one of the largest skulls found in any terrestrial animal, with the frill alone measuring approximately 2.8 meters in length.
Early measurements by John Bell Hatcher estimated the skull of the type specimen at 2.2 meters long, while a larger specimen reached 2.35 meters.

Individuals were comparable in size to the largest Triceratops specimens but were distinguished by an elongated frill with large fenestrae, long squamosal bones with a dorsal channel, and five or more pairs of epiparietal horns.
The primary difference between Torosaurus and Triceratops was the shape of their frills.
Despite common belief, the name Torosaurus does not mean 'bull lizard' but rather 'perforated lizard', derived from the ancient Greek word for perforated.
The name was likely derived from the Greek verb 'toreo,' meaning 'to perforate,' because the open perforations in the parietal bones suggested this unique feature to the describer.
A large specimen is considered a subadult because its unfused sutures and smooth bone texture indicate it was not fully grown despite its impressive size.
The genus Torosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1891.
In 1891, John Bell Hatcher discovered a pair of ceratopsian skulls with elongated, perforated frills in Niobrara County, southeastern Wyoming.
Marsh explained that the open perforations in the parietal bones suggested the name Torosaurus and separated it from other known ceratopsids.
Horner emphasized that ceratopsian frills consisted of metaplastic bone, which can lengthen and shorten over time by extending and reabsorbing to form new shapes.
Researchers consider the idea that Torosaurus frill holes formed after the bone was rejuvenated and granulated again to be an unlikely sequence.
The type species of the genus Torosaurus is Torosaurus latus, which is based on holotype YPM 1830, a partial skull.
The holotype for the species T. gladius was specimen YPM 1831, which is an even larger skull than the type species.
Torosaurus has traditionally been classified in the subfamily Chasmosaurinae due to its long frill, a grouping confirmed by cladistic analysis in the 1990s.
The genus belongs to the parent group Triceratopsini.
Torosaurus lived during the Late Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous period in North America, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Torosaurus have been found across the Western Interior of North America, ranging from Saskatchewan to Texas.
Both fossils were found in the Lance Formation, which dates to the Maastrichtian stage, though the genus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.

In 2010, a study suggested that Torosaurus might represent the mature growth stage of Triceratops, characterized by an elongated frill and holes appearing during maturation, a hypothesis supported by John Scannella in 2009 based on fossils in the Hell Creek Formation.
It is currently debated whether T. utahensis should be considered a distinct genus or the mature growth stage of a Triceratops species, similar to the hypothesis for T. latus.
In 1998, Thomas Lehman claimed that a Pentaceratops specimen had a skull that would have been 2.9 meters long in life.
